title: How a Filter Works
short_hook: Your charger does this 100 times a second.

scenes.title: HOW A FILTER WORKS
scenes.subtitle: From bumpy DC to smooth DC, cycle by cycle
scenes.narration: Your phone charger takes the wavy AC from the wall and turns it into calm, steady DC. But there's one part that does the real smoothing, and most students never see how it actually works. Today we'll watch it happen, cycle by cycle.

scenes.label: What a rectifier gives you
scenes.narration: Here's the problem. A rectifier flips the negative half of the AC wave upwards, so the current only flows one way. That's DC, technically. But look at it. It rises to the top and falls all the way to zero, again and again. We call this pulsating DC, and most electronics can't run on it.

scenes.title: The journey of power
items: Wall socket: 230 V AC, 50 cycles per second
Transformer: steps it down to about 12 V AC
Bridge rectifier: makes it flow one way
scenes.narration: So let's follow the full journey. The wall gives about two hundred and thirty volts of AC, fifty cycles every second. A transformer brings it down to around twelve volts. A bridge rectifier makes it flow in one direction. And then the filter, our hero today, smooths out the bumps.

First, the bridge rectifier. Four diodes, arranged in a loop, with the AC source in the middle and the load on the right. A diode is a one-way valve. Current can only go in the direction of the arrow. Watch one full AC cycle, slowed down. One cycle takes twenty milliseconds.

scenes.q: In the positive half-cycle, which two diodes switch on?
scenes.narration: Quick question before I show you. When the left side of the source is positive, which two diodes switch on? Pause and think. Three, two, one.

The answer is D1 and D2. The left side is positive, so current goes up through D1 to the plus rail, down through the load, and back through D2 to the source. Now look at the blue dots. Those are electrons, and they move the opposite way, from minus to plus. D3 and D4 are reverse biased, so they stay off.

Now the negative half-cycle. The right side of the source becomes positive. This time D3 and D4 conduct, and D1 and D2 switch off. Here's the clever part. The current still flows down through the load in the same direction. That's why the output only ever goes up, never below zero.

scenes.label: Two humps every cycle
scenes.narration: So every AC cycle gives us two humps, one from each half. At fifty hertz, that's one hundred humps every second. Between every hump, the voltage drops all the way to zero. If you powered a microcontroller like this, it would reset a hundred times a second. So how do we fill those gaps?

We add a capacitor. Think of it as a small, very fast rechargeable tank. It's just two metal plates with an insulator between them. When you connect a voltage, electrons pile up on one plate and are pulled away from the other. No current crosses the gap. The charge is simply stored.

And when the outside voltage drops, the capacitor gives that charge back. Electrons flow out of the minus plate, through the circuit, and back to the plus plate. So a capacitor charges when the voltage rises, and supplies power when the voltage falls. Remember that, because that's the entire trick.

Now we place the capacitor across the output, next to the load. Watch the first quarter cycle. As the input rises, D1 and D2 conduct. They feed the load, and at the same time they charge the capacitor, all the way up to the peak. With twelve volts AC, that peak is about fifteen and a half volts, after the two diode drops.

scenes.q: The input now starts falling. What happens to the output?
scenes.narration: Now the input starts falling back towards zero. What happens to the output voltage? Does it fall with the input, or does something hold it up? Think about it. Three, two, one.

The capacitor holds it up. The moment the input drops below the capacitor's voltage, the diodes become reverse biased and switch off. Now the capacitor alone feeds the load. It slowly discharges, and the voltage only dips a little, until the next half-cycle rises above it and tops it up again.

And that repeats every half-cycle. A short burst of charging at the top, then a longer stretch where the capacitor carries the load. The output is no longer a row of humps. It's almost flat, with a small wobble on top. That wobble is called ripple.

scenes.label: Small capacitor = big ripple
scenes.narration: The size of the ripple depends on the capacitor. A small capacitor stores little charge, so it drains quickly between peaks. The output dips a lot. That's a big ripple.

scenes.q: If we double the capacitor, the ripple becomes…
scenes.narration: So here's one for you. If we double the capacitor, keeping the same load, what happens to the ripple? Pause and think. Three, two, one.

scenes.label: Big capacitor = small ripple
scenes.narration: It drops to about half. A bigger capacitor stores more charge, so it barely drains before the next peak tops it up. The output is much smoother. That's why power supplies use such big filter capacitors.

Engineers use this simple formula. Ripple equals the load current divided by the ripple frequency times the capacitance. For a full-wave rectifier the frequency is one hundred hertz, two humps per cycle. So with one hundred milliamps and a thousand microfarads, you get about one volt of ripple. Use a twenty-two hundred microfarad capacitor, and it drops to under half a volt.

scenes.title: What you learned
items: A rectifier gives pulsating DC: 100 humps a second
Positive half: D1 + D2 · Negative half: D3 + D4
The capacitor charges at each peak
Between peaks, the diodes are OFF and C feeds the load
Bigger C or smaller load = less ripple
scenes.narration: Let's recap. The rectifier gives pulsating DC, a hundred humps a second. D1 and D2 handle the positive half, D3 and D4 the negative half. The capacitor charges at every peak, and between peaks the diodes switch off while the capacitor feeds the load. A bigger capacitor, or a smaller load, means less ripple.

scenes.title: FILTERS
scenes.narration: Next time, we'll see how a voltage regulator takes this slightly wobbly DC and makes it perfectly flat. Here's a question for the comments. Where else have you seen a big capacitor on a circuit board? Subscribe so you don't miss the next lesson.
